Lessons.Title: Relate Division and Multiplication
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: interpret the same equal-sharing situation as a quotient, a fraction, a mixed number and multiplication of a whole by a unit fraction. The relationship must be explained with the *same whole and unit* rather than selected only because two calculations match.

Warm-up — number talk: reason mentally about 3×1/2, 3×2/2, 3×3/2 and 5×3/2. Use a pair of half-sized strips for each whole and describe a half as one of two equal parts. A teacher compares the different methods and checks whether students justify their counting of halves.

Activity 1 — shared relay distance: two runners divide a three-mile relay into equal portions. Represent a three-mile segment split into two equal halves; each runner completes 3÷2=3/2=1 1/2 miles, also described as one-half of three miles or (1/2)×3. A learner draws and describes their own equal-length diagram; do not treat a correct number as proof the drawing shows equal distances.

Activity 2 — match the interpretation: read two independent strip descriptions. Model A uses three one-mile strips with one half of each shaded. Model B uses a three-mile strip cut into two equal pieces, one shaded. Show how both represent 3×1/2, 3÷2 and 1/2×3 even though the grouping of regions differs.

Source boundary: the public original lesson specifically asks children to explain diagram-expression correspondences, then revise writing after talking with several partners. The expression alone is a useful numeric check but partner explanation and diagrams require teacher review. Source images and gated Cool-down are not reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Quotient as a fraction
KeyConcepts.Definition: Dividing a positive whole quantity into b equal shares represents an a/b fraction.
KeyConcepts.Example: One runner in an equal two-person three-mile race covers 1 1/2 miles.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit fraction of a quantity
KeyConcepts.Definition: One of b equal shares of a quantity can be represented by multiplication.
KeyConcepts.Example: Half of three miles is (1/2)×3 miles=3/2 miles.

KeyConcepts.Title: Different diagrams, same amount
KeyConcepts.Definition: Dividing a whole strip into equal segments or combining fractions of identical unit strips can model one quantity.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Keep one common unit mile and count lengths rather than unrelated picture sizes.
KeyConcepts.Example: Three half-mile segments sum to 1 1/2 miles.

WorkedExamples.Title: Two-runner relay
WorkedExamples.Question: Two runners equally split a three-mile relay. How far does each travel?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction model with exact arithmetic; teacher judges the diagram and explanation.
Steps: Start with the full three-mile distance.
Partition the distance into two equal lengths.
Calculate 3÷2=3/2 and regroup as 1 1/2 miles.
WorkedExamples.Check: Two equal shares of 3/2 mile total three miles.

WorkedExamples.Title: Show two equivalent expressions
WorkedExamples.Question: Why do 3×(1/2) and 3÷2 give the same result in the relay situation?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction model with exact arithmetic; teacher judges the diagram and explanation.
Steps: Interpret 3×1/2 as three half-mile contributions.
Interpret 3÷2 as splitting three full miles into two equal distances.
Count each description as three halves of a mile.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare diagram descriptions
WorkedExamples.Question: Does half of each of three one-mile bars give the same distance as half of one three-mile bar?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction model with exact arithmetic; teacher judges the diagram and explanation.
Steps: In the first drawing, select a half-mile from each one-mile bar.
In the second, divide a three-mile segment by two to get 3/2.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks scale, unit lengths, equal areas and explanatory correspondence.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat the two runners as each running all three miles
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The relay distance is divided equally, not repeated twice.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Each portion is half of the team's three-mile total.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat the multiplication and division as unrelated answers
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: These operations describe the same partition under compatible unit conventions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Match each factor and divisor to an identified number of equal parts.

SummaryPoints: Dividing a whole by b is taking one b-th of that amount.
3÷2=3/2=1 1/2=(1/2)×3, with miles attached to the result.
Matching equal-unit strip diagrams and explaining relationships are teacher-reviewed.

Lessons.Title: Divide to Multiply Unit Fractions PLC Activity
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: find one-fourth of a whole-number road length using exact division, and connect multiplication by one-fourth to taking four equal shares. Students compare story, diagram and expressions, not merely calculate a decimal.

Warm-up — estimation exploration: locate a mark on a 0-to-5 number line that falls before 2 1/2 and propose low, reasonable and high estimates. The publisher's actual distance marker is not reproduced here; the first-party example gives the mark exactly at 1 3/4. This is about number-line magnitude, not identifying a universal location for an image not provided.

Activity 1 — two roads: Mai runs one-fourth of a nine-mile road and Han one-fourth of a seven-mile road. Model each complete road with four equal strips or with a labeled number line. Compute 9÷4=9/4=2 1/4 miles and 7÷4=7/4=1 3/4 miles, and explain why each result is one fourth of its original road.

Activity 2 — match representations: discuss how 7÷4, (1/4)×7 and 7/4 all describe the same one-fourth-of-seven amount. Construct a text or drawn area diagram and choose among candidate expressions; require a reason based on the diagram, not simply arithmetic coincidence.

Assessment: the original source includes a card-sorting partner routine with multiple diagram matches, questions and discussion. Source card images and protected teacher response are not reproduced. Numeric correctness is supporting evidence; strategy comparison, diagram construction and peer critique remain teacher-reviewed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit fraction of a road length
KeyConcepts.Definition: One fourth of a segment is one of four equal-length parts of that segment.
KeyConcepts.Rule: (1/4)×a = a÷4 = a/4 for an a-unit segment.
KeyConcepts.Example: One fourth of 9 miles is 9/4 miles.

KeyConcepts.Title: Improper fractions and mixed numbers
KeyConcepts.Definition: A fraction larger than one can be represented as complete units and a remaining fractional unit.
KeyConcepts.Example: Nine quarters make two whole miles and one quarter.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compare using a common benchmark
KeyConcepts.Definition: A unit fraction is an operator on a specified whole, so different wholes give different absolute fractions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: One fourth of nine is larger than one fourth of seven because nine is larger than seven.

WorkedExamples.Title: Quarter of nine miles
WorkedExamples.Question: Mai ran 1/4 of a nine-mile road. How far was the run?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction model with exact arithmetic; teacher judges the diagram and explanation.
Steps: Divide the whole nine-mile road into four equal segments.
Each part has length 9÷4=9/4 miles.
Regroup nine fourths into two wholes and one fourth.
WorkedExamples.Check: Four equal lengths of 9/4 mile total nine miles.

WorkedExamples.Title: Quarter of seven miles
WorkedExamples.Question: Han ran 1/4 of a seven-mile road. How far was the run?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction model with exact arithmetic; teacher judges the diagram and explanation.
Steps: Divide the seven-mile whole into four equal distances.
Find the single share: 7÷4=7/4 miles.
Convert to one whole plus three fourths.

WorkedExamples.Title: Three equivalent expressions
WorkedExamples.Question: Which expressions represent one fourth of seven miles: 7÷4, 1/4×7, or 7/4?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction model with exact arithmetic; teacher judges the diagram and explanation.
Steps: Read 7÷4 as one of four equal groups of seven.
Read 1/4×7 as one fourth of the full seven-mile length.
Read 7/4 as seven quarter-mile units; count to one and three quarters.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks that the learner's diagram uses equal lengths and a consistent seven-mile whole.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Take 1/4 mile regardless of road length
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: One fourth names a proportion of the entire given road, not a fixed physical length.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label the complete road before dividing it into four equal parts.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Equal sharing must retain fractional distance.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Record 7/4 miles exactly and explain the mixed number.

SummaryPoints: A quarter of a positive road length is the length divided by four.
Matching story, diagram and equivalent expressions requires teacher-reviewed justification.

Lessons.Title: Divide to Multiply Non-unit Fractions
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: relate a non-unit fraction of a whole number to a unit-fraction product and repeated equal parts. The original lesson emphasizes why the multiplication and division expressions can describe the same shaded model, including a whole-number value where the fraction is above one after multiplying.

Warm-up — true or false: reason about 2×(1/3×6)=2/3×6, 2×(1/3×6)=2×(6÷3), and the false claim that 2/3×6 equals 2×(1/4×6). Reject the last claim because it substitutes a different-sized unit fraction, even without fully computing both sides.

Activity 1 — build from one fifth: find (1/5)×3 as three fifths, then double it for (2/5)×3 = 6/5 and triple it for (3/5)×3 = 9/5. A partitioned bar model should show the same whole three units and the correct number of fifths; ask learners to explain how the number of shaded parts changes.

Activity 2 — expression matching: use three congruent one-unit bars each cut into five equal parts, with two fifths shaded on each. The total shaded amount is 3×(2/5)=6/5 units. Show why 2×(3÷5), 6/5, 3×(2/5), and 3×2×(1/5) all match that description. Label the equal-size parts, unit whole and relationship to division.

Teacher review: original diagram and source peer talk demand explaining the meaning of factors and fractions, not simply proving equality by a calculator. The independent bar descriptions supplement source teaching; original publisher image and protected Cool-down are not reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Non-unit fraction multiplication
KeyConcepts.Definition: A/b of a whole number selects a copies of one-b-th of the quantity.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit-fraction building blocks
KeyConcepts.Definition: A multiple of a unit fraction can be assembled into a non-unit fraction amount.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Twice one fifth of a whole quantity is two fifths of that quantity.
KeyConcepts.Example: If one fifth of three is 3/5, then two fifths of three is 6/5.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent shaded-region expressions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Several expressions can describe the same group of selected equal parts.
KeyConcepts.Example: Three groups of 2/5 contain six equal fifth-sized pieces.

WorkedExamples.Title: Build non-unit fraction from one-fifth
WorkedExamples.Question: Calculate 1/5, 2/5 and 3/5 of three whole units.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction model with exact arithmetic; teacher judges the diagram and explanation.
Steps: Partition each of the three unit bars into fifths.
Select one fifth of each bar, yielding 3/5 total.
Double and triple that selected amount without changing the original unit.
WorkedExamples.Check: The three totals contain three, six and nine equal fifth-unit pieces respectively.

WorkedExamples.Title: Match multiple multiplication and division expressions
WorkedExamples.Question: Explain why 2×(3÷5), 3×(2/5) and 6/5 represent the same quantity.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction model with exact arithmetic; teacher judges the diagram and explanation.
Steps: Find 3÷5=3/5 and double it to 6/5.
Find three copies of 2/5 and add them to 6/5.
Count six shaded fifths in a common whole-unit model.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks the diagram's unit equivalence and expression interpretation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject a false unit-fraction substitution
WorkedExamples.Question: Is 2×(1/3×6) equal to 2×(1/4×6)?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction model with exact arithmetic; teacher judges the diagram and explanation.
Steps: Identify that one third of six is two, while one fourth of six is one and a half.
Double the first amount to four; double the second amount to three.
Compare four and three to reject equality.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No: the left equals 4 and the right equals 3.
WorkedExamples.Check: The original fractions 1/3 and 1/4 select differently sized parts of six.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Add numerator and denominator when multiplying a fraction
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The number of selected equal parts multiplies, while their size remains one denominator-sized unit.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count the equal fifths explicitly or use a×(n÷b).

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat two different unit fractions as interchangeable
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: One third and one fourth divide the same whole into different part sizes.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep the denominator and unit whole fixed within each represented expression.

SummaryPoints: A non-unit fraction of a quantity can be built from multiple copies of a unit-fraction part.
Choosing and explaining a correct shaded diagram is teacher-reviewed, beyond numeric equality.
